title: What is HTTP/3 support in the JDK HttpClient (HttpClient.Version.HTTP_3), and why does QUIC improve connection setup and resilience?
shortTitle: What is HTTP/3 in JDK HttpClient?
keyPoints: HTTP/3 uses the QUIC protocol (UDP-based) instead of TCP for faster and more resilient connections
0-RTT connection setup combines transport and TLS handshake in one round-trip instead of three
No head-of-line blocking: each stream is independent, so one lost packet affects only its stream
Connection migration allows connections to survive network switches (WiFi to mobile) without re-establishing
Automatic fallback to HTTP/2 if the server does not support QUIC
Same request/response API: only the transport changes, not application code

s1_definition.oneliner: HTTP/3 in the JDK HttpClient uses the QUIC protocol (UDP-based) for 0-RTT connection setup, no head-of-line blocking, and connection migration across network changes.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **QUIC protocol** – a transport built on UDP that combines connection establishment and TLS handshake, typically completing in one round-trip.
- **0-RTT setup** – QUIC can resume connections with zero round-trips using cached parameters, versus TCP+TLS which needs three round-trips.
- **No head-of-line blocking** – HTTP/2 over TCP has one TCP stream; one lost packet stalls ALL HTTP streams. QUIC gives each HTTP stream its own independent transport stream.
- **Connection migration** – QUIC connections survive IP address changes (WiFi to mobile), unlike TCP which requires a new handshake.
- **JDK integration** – `HttpClient.Version.HTTP_3` requests QUIC, with automatic fallback to HTTP/2.
s1_definition.analogy: HTTP/2 over TCP is a single-lane bridge: one accident blocks all traffic. HTTP/3 over QUIC has multiple independent lanes: one accident only blocks that lane. Plus entering the bridge is faster (0-RTT) and you can switch bridges mid-journey without stopping (connection migration).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 Connection Setup:

  HTTP/2 (TCP + TLS):
  Client ──SYN──────────▶ Server       1 RTT
  Client ◀─SYN+ACK───── Server
  Client ──ACK──────────▶ Server       2 RTT (TCP done)
  Client ──TLS Hello───▶ Server       3 RTT (TLS done)
  Client ◀─TLS Done──── Server
  Client ──Request─────▶ Server       4 RTT (first request)

  HTTP/3 (QUIC):
  Client ──QUIC+TLS────▶ Server       1 RTT (combined!)
  Client ◀─Response──── Server
  Client ──Request─────▶ Server       (first request in 1 RTT)

  Resumption (0-RTT):
  Client ──Data────────▶ Server       0 RTT (cached params)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
HTTP/3 in the JDK HttpClient uses the QUIC protocol (UDP-based) for three improvements over HTTP/2. First, 0-RTT connection setup combines transport and TLS handshake in one round-trip instead of three. Second, no head-of-line blocking means one lost packet only affects its stream, not all streams on the connection. Third, connection migration allows connections to survive network changes without re-establishing.

The Java API is unchanged: same HttpClient, HttpRequest, and HttpResponse. You set `HttpClient.Version.HTTP_3` and the client negotiates QUIC with the server, falling back to HTTP/2 if unavailable. Application code does not change.

In banking microservices, HTTP/3 reduces inter-service latency (fewer round-trips for connection setup) and improves resilience on unreliable networks (mobile banking apps, cross-region calls). The benefit is most significant when connection setup cost and packet loss are the dominant latency contributors.

Remember one sentence: HTTP/3 uses QUIC for 0-RTT connection setup, no head-of-line blocking, and connection migration, while keeping the same Java HttpClient API.
